# Transformers 2:

This notebook is the "exercise sheet" for week 7 of the NLP lecture and will introduce you to deploying Transformers models using [Hugging Face](https://huggingface.co/$0). We will also look into visualising their characteristic attention mechanism and their contextualised embeddings.

Goals:
- getting comfortable with loading tokenisers and models from [HuggingFace]()
- look at the architecture of a transformer model
- try out some visualisation techniques for attention
- play around with contextualised word embeddings

On the top drop-down menu in Google Colab, go to Runtime → Change runtime type and select a GPU (e.g., T4).

**Recommendation**: Switch to a GPU only once your code is prepared. In the free version of Google Colab, GPU usage time is limited. If you enable a GPU runtime and leave it running for a long time while setting up your code, you may waste your compute units.

---

# Part A: Transformer Architecture
## 0. Imports
# Install required libraries (only needed on Colab or a fresh environment)
!pip install -q transformers bertviz torch gensim

import torch
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns
from bertviz import head_view, model_view

from transformers import AutoConfig, AutoTokenizer, AutoModelForSeq2SeqLM

import warnings
warnings.filterwarnings('ignore')

print('All libraries imported successfully!')
## 1. Loading models and tokenisers

* In the following experiment, we compare two models: a randomly initialized T5 model and trained T5 model
* Start by loading a randomly initialized T5 model
    * Make use of the imported `AutoConfig`
    * Specify `output_attentions=True`
* Repeat the process for pre-trained T5
    * For pre-trained T5, load ["google-t5/t5-small"](https://huggingface.co/google-t5/t5-small) using [AutoModelForSeq2SeqLM.from_pretrained](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/en/model_doc/auto#transformers.AutoModelForSeq2SeqLM.from_pretrained)
    * Also specify `output_attentions=True` for both
* Set all models into `eval()` mode

# loading an untrained (random/rnd) and a pretrained T5 model
model_name = "google-t5/t5-small"

# for the untrained model: get a generic T5-small model config
config = AutoConfig.from_pretrained(model_name, output_attentions=True)
rnd_t5 = AutoModelForSeq2SeqLM.from_config(config) # load the model
rnd_t5.eval() # set the model to eval mode (as opposed to training mode)

# load pretrained T5 model
t5 = AutoModelForSeq2SeqLM.from_pretrained(model_name, output_attentions=True)
t5.eval()
print("Models loaded!")

print(t5)

# load the pretrained t5 tokenizer using the AutoTokenizer class
# the syntax is very similar to t5 model loading (no output attentions, no .eval() mode needed)
tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_name)
## 2. Model Inference

Let's prepare a sentence to be passed to the model as input.

We need to:
1) tokenise, and
2) convert tokens to input IDs

# Let's start with an explicit example:

sentence = "The animal didn't cross the street because it was too tired."

# tokenize
tokens_raw = tokenizer.tokenize(sentence)

# add T5's special end of sequence token
tokens = tokens_raw + ["</s>"]

# convert tokens to token IDs
token_ids = tokenizer.convert_tokens_to_ids(tokens)

# here's what happened:
for x in zip (tokens_raw +[" ", " "], tokens+[" ", " "], token_ids):
  print(f"{x[0]:<8}-->{x[1]:>10}\t-->{x[2]:>6}")
Conveniently, the tokeniser can handle this for us in one simple "encode" step.

sentence = "The animal didn't cross the street because it was too tired."

# convert sentence to token ids
token_ids = tokenizer.encode(sentence, return_tensors='pt')

print(token_ids) # same as token_ids above

# To find out how the sentence was tokenised and what these numbers stand for, examine:
tok_names = tokenizer.convert_ids_to_tokens(token_ids[0])

for x in zip(token_ids[0], tok_names):
  print(x[0], "\t-->", x[1])

Time to pass the inputs to the models:
* Run the sequence through both models
    * Disable gradient calculation to save memory and speed up the process, because we do not want to train the models by backpropagation.
    * Extract and save the attention outputs

#for simplicity, we use the same token sequence for the decoder input as that of the encoder input
with torch.no_grad(): # disables gradients
  rnd_out = rnd_t5(input_ids=token_ids, decoder_input_ids=token_ids)

print(f' Decoder self-attention : {len(rnd_out.decoder_attentions)} layers')

# B: Visualising Attention

## 1. Nodes and Arches per Layer and Head

* Visualize the attention maps using [`bertviz`](https://github.com/jessevig/bertviz$0)'s [model_view](https://github.com/jessevig/bertviz#model-view) and [head_view](https://github.com/jessevig/bertviz#head-view) for each of the two models
* Inspect the attention patterns and structures by hovering over/clicking on the graphics
* If you encounter a `javascript: require is not defined` error, simply execute the cell again, sometimes jupyterlab's widgets need to be reloaded

# untrained model (encoder attentions)
model_view(encoder_attention=rnd_out.encoder_attentions,
          decoder_attention=rnd_out.decoder_attentions,
          cross_attention=rnd_out.cross_attentions,
           encoder_tokens=tok_names,
           decoder_tokens=tok_names)
head_view(rnd_out.encoder_attentions, tok_names) # you can also set other attentions!
Compelte the code and compare this to the trained T5 model:
model_view(...)
head_view(...)

What general differences do you notice between:
- the untrained and trained T5 models?
- the encoder vs decoder attention?

your answer: ...

## 2. Attention Heatmaps on Grids

Each **row** = a query token (the token being processed).  
Each **column** = a key token (the token being attended to).  
Colour intensity = attention weight — brighter means more attention.

Each row sums to **1** (it is a probability distribution).

> Change `LAYER` (0–5) and `HEAD` (0–7) to explore different specialisations.

# Change these to explore!
LAYER = 3   # 0 = first layer, 5 = last layer
HEAD  = 5   # 0 to 7

# extract attention layers
t5_encoder_attention = t5_out.encoder_attentions
t5_decoder_attention = t5_out.decoder_attentions

attn_matrix = t5_encoder_attention[LAYER].squeeze(0)[HEAD].numpy()

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 8))
sns.heatmap(
    attn_matrix,
    xticklabels=tokens,
    yticklabels=tokens,
    cmap='viridis',
    vmin=0, vmax=1, # fixed scale of 0-1 since we are looking at a probability space
    linewidths=0.4, linecolor='#e0e0e0',
    ax=ax,
    cbar_kws={'label': 'Attention weight', 'shrink': 0.7}
)
ax.set_title(f'Attention Weights — Layer {LAYER}, Head {HEAD}',
             fontsize=14, fontweight='bold', pad=16)
ax.set_xlabel('Key tokens  (attended TO)', fontsize=11)
ax.set_ylabel('Query tokens  (processing FROM)', fontsize=11)
ax.tick_params(axis='x', rotation=45, labelsize=10)
ax.tick_params(axis='y', rotation=0,  labelsize=10)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

print('Tip: try Layer 0 Head 0 for positional patterns,')
print('     or later layers for more semantic relationships.')

---
## Comparing all 8 heads in one layer

Each head learns to attend to different things.
This panel lets you compare all 8 heads in a single layer at a glance.

**What to look for:**
- Some heads attend strongly to the **diagonal** (each token looks mostly at itself or neighbours)
- Some heads show strong attention to `</s>`
- Some heads capture **syntactic** or **coreference** relationships

> Change `LAYER_TO_SHOW` to inspect a different layer.

LAYER_TO_SHOW = 5

num_heads = t5.config.num_attention_heads
# looking at the ENCODER here
all_heads = t5_encoder_attention[LAYER_TO_SHOW].squeeze(0).numpy()  # size: (8, tokens, tokens)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(3, 3, figsize=(14, 14))
fig.suptitle(f'All {num_heads} Attention Heads — Layer {LAYER_TO_SHOW}',
             fontsize=16, fontweight='bold', y=1.01)

for head_idx, ax in enumerate(axes.flat):
    sns.heatmap(
        all_heads[head_idx],
        xticklabels=tokens,
        yticklabels=tokens,
        cmap='Reds', vmin=0, vmax=1,
        ax=ax, cbar=False,
        linewidths=0.2, linecolor='#ebebeb'
    )
    ax.set_title(f'Head {head_idx}', fontsize=10, fontweight='bold')
    ax.tick_params(axis='x', rotation=45, labelsize=6)
    ax.tick_params(axis='y', rotation=0,  labelsize=6)
    ax.set_xlabel('')
    ax.set_ylabel('')

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

# you can ignore the IndexError, it's only because of the plotting mismatch
## 3. Mean Attention Scores per Token

TOKEN_OF_INTEREST = 'it'
LAYER_FOR_TOKEN   = 4


query_idx =  tokens.index((tokens[0][0] # prepend special ▁ whitespace character (is not the standard underscore!)
                           +TOKEN_OF_INTEREST if not TOKEN_OF_INTEREST in tokens else TOKEN_OF_INTEREST))


# again, currently set to ENCODER
layer_attn   = t5_encoder_attention[LAYER_FOR_TOKEN].squeeze(0).numpy()  # (heads, tokens, tokens)
mean_attn_row = layer_attn[:, query_idx, :].mean(axis=0)       # (tokens,)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(12, 4))
colors = ['#DC2626' if (t == TOKEN_OF_INTEREST or t[1:] == TOKEN_OF_INTEREST) else '#2563EB' for t in tokens]
bars = ax.bar(tokens, mean_attn_row, color=colors, edgecolor='white', linewidth=0.5)

ax.set_title(
    f'Attention paid BY "{TOKEN_OF_INTEREST}" TO each token'
    f' (Layer {LAYER_FOR_TOKEN}, avg over all encoder heads)',
    fontsize=13, fontweight='bold'
)
ax.set_ylabel('Mean attention weight', fontsize=11)
ax.set_xlabel('Token', fontsize=11)
ax.tick_params(axis='x', rotation=45, labelsize=10)

for bar, val in zip(bars, mean_attn_row):
    ax.text(
        bar.get_x() + bar.get_width() / 2,
        bar.get_height() + 0.002,
        f'{val:.3f}', ha='center', va='bottom', fontsize=8, color='#333'
    )

ax.spines[['top', 'right']].set_visible(False)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

top3 = np.argsort(mean_attn_row)[::-1][:3]
print(f'\nTop 3 tokens attended to by "{TOKEN_OF_INTEREST}":')
for rank, idx in enumerate(top3, 1):
    print(f'  {rank}. "{tokens[idx]}"  ->  {mean_attn_row[idx]:.4f}')

TOKEN_OF_INTEREST = 'it'
LAYER_FOR_TOKEN   = 4


query_idx =  tokens.index((tokens[0][0] # prepend special ▁ whitespace character (is not standard underscore!)
                           +TOKEN_OF_INTEREST if not TOKEN_OF_INTEREST in tokens else TOKEN_OF_INTEREST))

# here we look at the DECODER
layer_attn   = t5_decoder_attention[LAYER_FOR_TOKEN].squeeze(0).numpy()  # (heads, tokens, tokens)
mean_attn_row = layer_attn[:, query_idx, :].mean(axis=0)       # (tokens,)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(12, 4))
colors = ['#DC2626' if (t == TOKEN_OF_INTEREST or t[1:] == TOKEN_OF_INTEREST) else '#2563EB' for t in tokens]
bars = ax.bar(tokens, mean_attn_row, color=colors, edgecolor='white', linewidth=0.5)

ax.set_title(
    f'Attention paid BY "{TOKEN_OF_INTEREST}" TO each token'
    f' (Layer {LAYER_FOR_TOKEN}, avg over all decoder heads)',
    fontsize=13, fontweight='bold'
)
ax.set_ylabel('Mean attention weight', fontsize=11)
ax.set_xlabel('Token', fontsize=11)
ax.tick_params(axis='x', rotation=45, labelsize=10)

for bar, val in zip(bars, mean_attn_row):
    ax.text(
        bar.get_x() + bar.get_width() / 2,
        bar.get_height() + 0.002,
        f'{val:.3f}', ha='center', va='bottom', fontsize=8, color='#333'
    )

ax.spines[['top', 'right']].set_visible(False)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

top3 = np.argsort(mean_attn_row)[::-1][:3]
print(f'\nTop 3 tokens attended to by "{TOKEN_OF_INTEREST}":')
for rank, idx in enumerate(top3, 1):
    print(f'  {rank}. "{tokens[idx]}"  ->  {mean_attn_row[idx]:.4f}')

# Part C: Contextualised Embeddings

In this section, we are going to compare contextualized embeddings from google-t5/t5-small with glove-wiki-gigaword-100. T5 is an encoder-decoder model based on the Transformer architecture, while GloVe is a static word embedding model from our Week 4 assignment.

GloVe is similar to word2vec but the training method is a little different in that GloVe optimizes the word vectors to fit the logarithm of their coocurance counts. We use gensim library to load the pretrained model.

https://github.com/piskvorky/gensim-data

https://nlp.stanford.edu/projects/glove


Now we want to compare the embeddings produced by GloVe and T5 using the sentence:
"that that that that student wrote on the blackboard is wrong.”
